after.abstract: Background Mental health problems among young people impose a burden extending beyond healthcare, including impaired health-related quality of life and high societal costs from disrupted education, lost productivity, and informal care. Youth-friendly interventions may reduce this burden by providing early support and preventing escalation. However, their broader societal economic impact remains insufficiently explored. Evaluations incorporating consequences beyond healthcare and longer time horizons can better capture their societal value. Methods This protocol outlines harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of YEAH, SELFIE, and MOST, three mental health interventions for young people aged 12-25. Each intervention will be compared separately against care as usual over 12 months, with longer-term costs and outcomes projected at 2, 3, 5, and 10 years. Multicountry participant data will be pooled, using a prespecified reference country for base-case costing and methodological guidance. A harmonised, context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument was developed to capture healthcare and broader societal resource use consistently across participating countries and to support evaluation of the economic impact of youth mental health interventions from a multicountry perspective. Uncertainty will be assessed through sensitivity and scenario analyses. Discussion The proposed harmonised methodological framework will support consistent estimation of the short- and long-term cost-effectiveness of three youth-friendly mental health interventions. It will enable comparison of intervention-specific results generated using different trial designs and support consistent estimation of costs and outcomes across the three interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument will further support consistent measurement of healthcare utilisation, productivity losses, and informal care across the economic evaluations. Conclusion By integrating trial-based evidence with long-term modelling and standardised measurement of resource use, this study aims to generate robust, policy-relevant evidence to inform health technology assessment and decision-making for youth mental health interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument is also intended to support future economic evaluations of mental health interventions conducted across multiple countries.

after.authors: Ekenze, O.; Banerjee, A.; Lioutas, V.-A.; Himali, D.; Seshadri, S.; Romero, J. R.; Aparicio, H. J.; Beiser, A. S.; Salinas, J.
after.abstract: Psychosocial factors are promising candidates as modifiable risk factors for stroke. Loneliness is of interest given its rising prevalence worldwide; yet the temporal relationship of loneliness with subsequent stroke remains unclear. Aim: To clarify the association between timing of loneliness and incident stroke. Methods: Framingham Heart Study participants free of stroke with at least two assessments of loneliness prior to incident stroke (at baseline exam, and at prior exam up to 15 years before baseline) were included. Loneliness was assessed using response to the I felt lonely item on the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, defined as feeling lonely for 3 days within the past week. The recency of loneliness was defined as prior loneliness (present at the prior exam) and baseline loneliness (present at the baseline exam). The primary analysis tested separately for associations between prior loneliness vs no prior loneliness, baseline versus no baseline loneliness, and incident stroke, with 15 years of follow up. Cox models were adjusted for age and sex (model 1) and additionally vascular risk factors (model 2), depressive symptoms (model 3), and physical activity (model 4). Interactions between loneliness and age and sex were explored. Results: Among 4307 participants (mean age 62{+/-}10 years, 55% women), 198 (4.5%) had an incident stroke over a median 6.5-year follow-up period. Prior loneliness was reported by 177 (4.1%) and 226 (5.2%) reported baseline loneliness. Compared to participants without prior loneliness, those with prior loneliness had nearly 3-fold increase in stroke risk after adjustment for age, sex, vascular risk factors, depressive symptoms, and physical activity (HR=2.85, 95% [CI] 1.51-5.39). The effect was primarily observed in participants <80 years (mean age 60 years.HR=3.21, 95% CI 1.69-6.13). No increased risk of stroke was observed among participants with loneliness at baseline. Conclusion: Our findings support consideration of loneliness as a potentially modifiable risk factor, particularly in midlife, for incident stroke.

after.abstract: Background: Variation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs. We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality. Methods: We assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS). Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing. Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK. Results: During a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred. Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95). Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in ?30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus. Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales, an order in which butyrate production has been reported. Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health. Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans. No associations were observed with ischemic stroke. Conclusions: Gut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

after.abstract: Background: The gut microbiome is an emerging risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD). Methods: We tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across four large prospective Nordic cohorts with 635 incident CVD in 11,604 participants in the discovery cohort and 2,309 incident CVD in 20,965 participants combined across three replication cohorts. Results: Higher Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a lower risk of incident CVD. In addition, the relative abundance of nine species and eleven bacterial functional modules showed reproducible associations with incident CVD in the discovery cohort and in a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts. We identified a female-specific gut microbiota-related pathway involving the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, enriched among denture users, thus serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health. Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal effect of denture use on increased relative abundance of Rothia mucilaginosa_A. This pathway was linked to increased CVD risk through altered gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating imidazole propionate levels, and increased levels of systemic inflammation biomarkers. The second pathway involved both ?-diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of metabolic syndrome and with bacterial pathways related to purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched chain amino acid biosynthesis. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways provide new insights into the underlying biology of CVD. Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and cardiovascular disease may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

after.title: Preprint: Aging, Structural, and Neighborhood-Environmental Correlates of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Factor Burden Across U.S. Census Tracts
after.authors: Batobara, A.; Alfaraidhy, M.; Tanriover, B.; Liu, Y.; Damluji, A. A.; Vest, A. R.; Lim, C.
after.abstract: Background. The American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions. Methods. We built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcome's BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates. Results. Agreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Moran's I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults 65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary model's residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both. Conclusions. CKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment.

after.authors: Eberle, R. B.; Rijhwani, H.; Tern, C.; Cho, M. H.; Saferali, A.
after.abstract: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung function are highly heritable, but for most genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci, the effector gene and the lung cell type in which it acts are unknown. Single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) offer a way to resolve the cell types in which regulatory variants act. Results: We integrated a multi-ancestry GWAS of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC; Shrine et al., n = 588,452) with single-cell lung eQTLs across 38 cell types (Natri et al., n = 114) by colocalization. We identified 20 candidate colocalizations (posterior probability of a shared causal variant > 0.7) for 13 genes in nine cell types, predominantly epithelial and immune. The two strongest signals localized DSP, an established COPD effector gene, and NRP2, a candidate effector gene, to alveolar type 2 epithelial cells; only these two colocalizations remained supported under a more conservative shared-effect prior. Both signals, together with FAM13A, were also detectable in bulk lung eQTLs, whereas most remaining loci colocalized only in the single-cell analysis. Conclusions: Single-cell eQTL colocalization resolves the alveolar epithelium as a cellular context for DSP and nominates NRP2 as a candidate lung function effector gene in the same compartment, highlighting the additional cellular resolution provided by single-cell data. The remaining candidate colocalizations warrant replication.

after.authors: Yum, Y.; Ogundairo, J.; Adeniji, F. P.; Nyirenda, G.; Udofia, P. I.; Kyung, S. E.; Ogunleye, V. O.; Siribie, M.; Mogeni, O.; Popoola, O.; Jeon, H.; Tadesse, B. T.; Okeke, I. N.; Marks, F.; Lee, J.-S.; Kehinde, A.
after.abstract: Background: Evidence on the economic burden of typhoid fever remains limited in sub-Saharan Africa. This study estimated the costs associated with typhoid fever and related invasive Salmonella infections in Ibadan, Nigeria. Methods: A field-based cost-of-illness study was conducted at six healthcare facilities between 2022 and 2025. Patients with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi), Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi (S. Paratyphi), invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS), or typhoid gastrointestinal perforation (special cases) were enrolled, with malaria patients serving as controls. Direct medical, direct non-medical, and indirect costs were estimated for each episode and converted from Nigerian naira to US dollars using year-specific exchange rates for 2022-2025. Cases and controls were matched by age group, sex, and point of care, and confidence intervals were estimated using non-parametric bootstrapping. Results: Among 198 participants, 69 were S. Typhi cases, one was S. Paratyphi case, 14 were iNTS cases, 12 were special cases, and 102 were malaria controls. Average total costs per episode were $130 for S. Typhi, $27 for S. Paratyphi, $156 for iNTS, $583 for special (perforation) cases, and $52 for malaria. For S. Typhi, costs were substantially higher among inpatients than outpatients ($309 vs. $72). Compared with matched malaria controls, the mean incremental total costs were $42 (95% CI: 18-71) for S. Typhi, $104 (95% CI: 25-197) for iNTS, and $560 (95% CI: 289-882) for special (perforation) cases. Conclusions: Typhoid fever imposes a considerable economic burden in Ibadan, Nigeria, particularly among patients requiring hospitalization or experiencing severe complications. These findings provide locally relevant evidence for evaluating typhoid conjugate vaccine introduction and informing resource-allocation decisions.

Methods: A field-based cost-of-illness study was conducted at six healthcare facilities between 2022 and 2025. Patients with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi), Salmonella enterica serovar Paratyphi (S. Paratyphi), invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS), or typhoid gastrointestinal perforation (special cases) were enrolled, with malaria patients serving as controls. Direct medical, direct non-medical, and indirect costs were estimated for each episode and converted from Nigerian naira to US dollars using year-specific exchange rates for 2022-2025. Cases and controls were matched by age group, sex, and point of care, and confidence intervals were estimated using non-parametric bootstrapping. Results: Among 198 participants, 69 were S. Typhi cases, one was S. Paratyphi case, 14 were iNTS cases, 12 were special cases, and 102 were malaria controls. Average total costs per episode were $130 for S. Typhi, $27 for S. Paratyphi, $156 for iNTS, $583 for special (perforation) cases, and $52 for malaria. For S. Typhi, costs were substantially higher among inpatients than outpatients ($309 vs. $72). Compared with matched malaria controls, the mean incremental total costs were $42 (95% CI: 18-71) for S. Typhi, $104 (95% CI: 25-197) for iNTS, and $560 (95% CI: 289-882) for special (perforation) cases. Conclusions: Typhoid fever imposes a considerable economic burden in Ibadan, Nigeria, particularly among patients requiring hospitalization or experiencing severe complications. after.authors: Batista Nunes Bandeira, T.; Gonzalez, A.; Poellabauer, C.; Mondal, A. M.
after.abstract: Objective: To develop and internally validate a calibrated discharge model of 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults, and to quantify how a future-information leak and outcome artifacts distorted performance, timing, and subgroup conclusions. Materials and Methods: Retrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV v3.1 admissions (87,750 patients; prevalence 21.4%). Predictors were audited for discharge-time availability; history features were tested for future information and recomputed from raw timestamps. A consensus gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model was selected inside patient-grouped folds; CIs used patient-cluster bootstrap. Results: A feature documented as a prior 180-day length-of-stay trend used each patient's whole record, including later admissions; removing it and two derived terms lowered test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.774 to 0.706. The corrected procedure reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.7057 (95% CI 0.7016 to 0.7102; primary); the 44-feature model scored 0.7056 on the historically exposed test partition (calibration slope 0.99), above reconstructed LACE and HOSPITAL (both P<.001). A day-1 discrimination peak largely reflected 2,368 probable administrative continuations within 1 hour of discharge; merging these into the preceding stay gave test AUROC 0.698 (0.702 after refitting). The White minus Black AUROC difference was 0.003 (95% CI -0.018 to 0.024); specificity was lower for Black patients (0.61 vs 0.69). Discussion: Documentation audits and patient-grouped validation missed a leak that inflated discrimination and created spurious subgroup and calendar-period differences; simple empirical checks found it. Conclusion: Empirical leakage checks should accompany availability audits. The corrected model is calibrated, moderately discriminating, and needs external validation before clinical use.

after.title: Preprint: Health professionals perceptions of human resource management practices and associated workplace factors in public hospitals of Gamo Zone, southern Ethiopia: A cross-sectional study
after.authors: Hailegiorgis, E. A.; Bateno, T.; Mekene, T.; Tunje, A.
after.abstract: Health workforce shortages in sub-Saharan Africa are compounded by how existing staff are managed, yet little quantitative evidence describes how hospital health professionals in Ethiopia perceive human resource management (HRM) practices or which workplace conditions accompany those perceptions. Drawing on social exchange theory, we assessed health professionals perceptions of HRM practices and their associations with workplace "cost" factors (job demands) and "benefit" factors (job resources) in public hospitals of Gamo Zone, southern Ethiopia. We conducted an institution-based cross-sectional survey from 15 February to 15 March 2025 in three of the zones six public hospitals, selected by lottery. Randomly sampled health professionals completed a structured questionnaire on tablets. Perception of HRM practices was measured with 28 five-point items covering seven practice domains and summarized as a mean score from 1 to 5; a mean above 3.0 was classified as a favorable perception. Associations were estimated with multivariable linear regression using heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors, adjusting for age, sex, profession and hospital. After removal of 41 duplicate records and 52 ineligible non-health staff, 343 health professionals were analyzed. The mean HRM perception score was 2.81 (standard deviation 0.58), and 29.0% (99/341; 95% confidence interval [CI] 24.5-34.1%) of participants held a favorable perception. Recruitment and training and development were rated least favorably, and selection most favorably. The proportion with a favorable perception ranged from 1.5% at the general hospital to 55.5% at one primary hospital. In the adjusted model (n = 326; R{superscript 2} = 0.46), greater perceived autonomy ({beta} = 0.20 per scale point; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.35) and recognition ({beta} = 0.12; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.22) were independently associated with more favorable perceptions. Skill ambiguity, work-life role conflict, schedule variability and interpersonal conflict were associated with less favorable perceptions in unadjusted analyses, but no cost factor remained independently associated after adjustment (joint test p = 0.459). Fewer than one in three health professionals viewed HRM practices favorably, with large differences between hospitals. Perceived recognition and autonomy, rather than job demands, were the workplace factors most consistently associated with how staff appraised HRM. These findings point to hospital-level management and non-financial job resources as priorities for health workforce governance research and practice in comparable low-resource settings.

after.title: Preprint: Determinants of Condom Use Among Sexually Active Men in a High-HIV-Burden Municipality in Ghana
after.authors: Appiah, P. Y.; Tettey, R. B.; Ortega-Santos, C. P.; Shine, J.; Manortey, S.
after.abstract: Consistent and correct condom use remains one of the most effective strategies for preventing sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, yet the determinants of male condom use are poorly documented at the district level in Ghana. This mixed-methods, cross-sectional study examined individual, sociocultural, and environmental determinants of condom use among 314 sexually active men aged 15 to 59 years, surveyed in 2016 in the Lower Manya Krobo Municipality, a district with historically elevated HIV prevalence (11.6% at its urban antenatal sentinel site in 2013; district population prevalence estimated at 5.56% in 2019). Data were collected via a structured questionnaire (quantitative) and two focus group discussions with eight participants (qualitative). In the final multivariable logistic regression model, having children was the only factor independently associated with ever having used a condom (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 95% confidence interval 1.74 to 6.19, p<0.001); age group, marital status, community of residence, and religion are not reported as adjusted estimates because their values were unstable in the presence of sparse cells. In the focus group discussions, younger men described pregnancy prevention rather than disease avoidance as their main motivation for condom use, while religious belief and social stigma (55.4% agreeing condom use is immoral, 58.3% citing partner-suspicion stigma) emerged as persistent barriers to acceptability. A gap between high awareness of condom effectiveness (77.1%) and frequent self-reported slippage or breakage (65.2% of ever-users) suggested a skills rather than a knowledge deficit. Although the data are a decade old, the normative and religious barriers recur in more recent national surveys, and the district remains comparatively high-burden, suggesting continued programmatic relevance. HIV and STI prevention programming for Ghanaian men may be more effective when framed within a broader sexual and reproductive health and family-planning context, engaging religious and community leaders directly and incorporating hands-on condom-use skills training rather than risk-based knowledge messaging alone.

after.title: Preprint: Shifting source hubs and the factors associated with cross-country Zika virus transmission: a phylogeographic network analysis, 2012-2025
after.authors: Pang, M.; Bu, X.; Liu, Q.; Li, C.; Chan, N.; Ji, H.; Qi, X.; Huang, Y.
after.abstract: Background Zika virus local transmission has been reported in at least 97 countries and territories, but the sources, routes, and determinants of cross-country spread remain incompletely understood. We reconstructed a phylogeographic network, characterized source activity across epidemic phases, and examined factors associated with identified cross-country transmission events. Methodology/Principal Findings We analyzed a time-scaled Nextstrain phylogeny of 1,043 Zika virus genomes collected between February 2013 and March 2026. Parent-child branches assigned to different locations were screened and consolidated into 81 source-destination-year events involving 39 locations. Network analysis characterized temporal and geographic patterns, routes, hubs, and communities. For the analysis of associated factors, 68 events with complete covariate data were compared, using mixed-effects models, with eligible year-matched control records for which no event was identified, with all 68 events retained and a new control set drawn in each of 200 iterations. Asia contributed the earliest event, from Thailand in 2012. Most events occurred within the Americas (79.0%) and were concentrated during 2014-2016, with Brazil as the principal source hub. All six events from 2019 onward originated from Thailand or India and reached destinations in Asia, Europe, and Africa. Thailand's source activity spanned 2012-2025. Event identification was positively associated with high source-country incidence (odds ratio [OR], 2.66; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.39-9.69), greater air travel (OR, 2.52; 95% CI, 1.58-5.67), and higher destination-country GNI per capita (OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.20-4.50). It was negatively associated with greater geographic distance (OR, 0.11; 95% CI, 0.02-0.20) and higher source-country GNI per capita (OR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.45-0.94). Fourteen source countries showed elevated residual source propensities, with Brazil and Thailand among the highest. Conclusions/Significance The transmission network showed a shift in dominant source hubs, from early activity in Asia to the Americas during the 2014-2016 epidemic and back to Asia in recent years. High source-country incidence, greater air travel, and shorter distance can help identify country pairs requiring closer surveillance, alongside established routes in the Americas and persistent or emerging Asian sources, particularly as El Nino may increase vector-borne transmission potential in 2026-2027.

after.title: Preprint: Maternal and Neonatal Outcomes Associated with Prenatal Prescription Stimulant Treatment Among Pregnant Individuals with Opioid Use Disorder
after.authors: Reese, T.; Leech, A. A.; Phillippi, J. C.; Patrick, S.; McNeer, E.; Loch, S.; Young, J.; von Horn, A.; Shah, M. V.; Wiese, A. D.
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction: Clinicians and Medicaid programs must decide whether to continue prescription stimulants in pregnancies complicated by opioid use disorder (OUD), yet no safety evidence exists for this population and stimulant coverage is frequently restricted. We evaluated maternal and neonatal outcomes associated with prescription stimulant treatment during pregnancy among individuals with OUD, including those with co-occurring stimulant use disorder (StUD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of Medicaid-insured pregnant individuals in Tennessee (2010-2021) with OUD. Our exposure of interest was any prescription amphetamine- or methylphenidate-class stimulant overlapping pregnancy. The primary maternal outcome was overdose from delivery through 1 year postpartum; secondary outcomes included death, severe maternal morbidity and cardiovascular complications in the first 6 weeks postpartum. The primary neonatal outcome was preterm birth; secondary outcomes included low birth weight, NICU admission, neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS), and death. We used overlap weighting to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and predicted probabilities and evaluated effect modification by buprenorphine. Results: Among 12,327 pregnancies with OUD, 380 (3.1%) received prescription stimulants during pregnancy; stimulant treated individuals were slightly older and more likely to have mental health comorbidities. In adjusted analyses, stimulant treatment was not associated with postpartum overdose (aOR, 1.13; 95% CI, 0.61-2.08), preterm birth (aOR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.74-1.46), cardiovascular complications, severe maternal morbidity, low birth weight, or NOWS. Odds of NICU admission were higher among stimulant exposed infants (aOR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.17-2.14). Maternal and infant deaths were rare. In exploratory analyses, overdose odds were elevated among pregnancies receiving both stimulants and buprenorphine (P for interaction = .03) and the cardiovascular composite was elevated within the ADHD subgroup (aOR, 2.33; 95% CI, 1.13-4.82). Conclusions: These first OUD-specific estimates do not support routine discontinuation of clinically indicated stimulant therapy in pregnancy. Higher NICU admission among stimulant-exposed infants, unaccompanied by differences in preterm birth, low birth weight, gestational age, or NOWS, is more consistent with intensified surveillance than with neonatal harm. Two exploratory signals require replication before they can inform practice.

after.title: Preprint: Feasibility of AI-Guided Handheld Echocardiography for Rheumatic Heart Disease Screening by Non-Cardiologists in Rural Nepal: A Mixed-Methods Diagnostic Accuracy Study
after.authors: Alattar, H.; Magesh, D.; Pal, A.; Mureau-Haines, R.; Young, T.; Ronen, K.; Zhang, D.; Pal, J.
after.abstract: Background: Rheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality in rural Nepal, where access to cardiovascular specialists and echocardiography is limited. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of AI-guided echocardiography performed by nurse practitioners for community-based RHD screening. Methods: We conducted a triangulation mixed-methods study (QUAN > qual) combining a paired cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study with semi-structured interviews during community screening camps in Damak, Nepal, in November 2025. Nurse practitioners performed AI-guided handheld echocardiography using EchoNous Kosmos Plus devices, with cardiologist overread serving as the comparator. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and kappa. Interviews were analyzed thematically. Results: Of 90 participants enrolled, 76 were included in the final analysis. Mean age was 50.8 years, 57.8% were male, and 42.2% had undergone prior cardiac evaluation. Detection of any valvular lesion demonstrated 95.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with near-perfect agreement with cardiologist interpretation (?=0.97). Lesion-specific performance included mitral regurgitation sensitivity 66.7% and specificity 97.3% (?=0.55), mitral stenosis sensitivity 100% and specificity 97.2% (?=0.81), aortic regurgitation sensitivity 90.9% and specificity 96.9% (?=0.84), and tricuspid regurgitation sensitivity and specificity of 100% (?=1.00). Mean scan duration was 5.8 minutes. Portability, AI-assisted acquisition, and remote review facilitated implementation, while training needs, workflow constraints, and technical issues were barriers. Conclusions: AI-guided handheld echocardiography performed by nurses demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and feasibility for rural RHD screening. AI-assisted task-shifting may expand access to early RHD detection in underserved settings.

after.authors: Potts, K. S.; Kianersi, S.; Faquih, T.; Noordam, R.; Rutter, M. K.; Sofer, T.; Cain, S.; Windred, D.; Burns, A. C.; Phillips, A. J. K.; Redline, S.; Wang, H.; Huang, T.
after.abstract: Background: Irregular sleep patterns are common and have been associated with higher cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of CVD, but evidence linking irregular sleep to hypertension is inconsistent. The objective of this study was to quantify associations between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study among 55,572 UK Biobank participants without hypertension or anti-hypertensive medication use who provided 5 valid days of accelerometry in 2013-2015 (60% women, mean age 61 years). We measured sleep regularity using the intra-individual standard deviation (SD) of sleep duration and the sleep regularity index (SRI), a measure of the similarity of sleep-wake patterns from one day to the next. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for incident hypertension, identified through linked health records, by levels of sleep regularity adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors as well as employment schedule. We also evaluated differences by demographic, clinical, and sleep-related (defined by duration, efficiency, timing, and sleep disorders) subgroups, and interaction with genetic susceptibility to hypertension. Results: During 7.9 years of follow-up, 5,713 participants developed hypertension. Participants with sleep duration SD >90 minutes had an 18% higher risk of incident hypertension compared to those with sleep duration SD 30 minutes (HR: 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06, 1.31). Similarly, participants in the lowest SRI quintile had a 40% higher risk than those in the highest SRI quintile (HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.52). These associations were generally consistent across demographic, health, and sleep-defined subgroups. Sleep irregularity and genetic susceptibility contributed independently to hypertension risk, without evidence of interaction. Conclusions: Irregular sleep patterns were associated with higher incident hypertension risk independent of established risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Maintaining regular sleep schedules may represent a modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention.

after.authors: Ghani, M. U.; Chang, H.; Shuhag, S.; Kamath, S.; Chughtai, S.; Bhuiyan, M. A. N.; Rodriguez, C. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Corewell Health Grand Rapids Hospitals - Butterworth
after.abstract: Background: Whether diabetes modified pandemic-related changes in cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality remains uncertain. We examined differential changes in US CVD mortality among deaths with versus without diabetes documented on the death certificate. Methods: We analyzed CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death data from 2005 to 2024, identifying deaths with CVD as the underlying cause among adults aged 25 years. Cohorts were CVD deaths with diabetes documented as a contributing cause (CVD+DM) and CVD deaths without documented diabetes. Because pre-2020 trajectories differed, the primary comparison of age-adjusted rates used a comparative interrupted time-series model allowing cohort-specific pre-2020 trends. Difference-in-differences estimates (2015-2019 vs 2020-2024) were descriptive. Results: CVD+DM mortality declined from 43.1 per 100,000 in 2005 to 34.3 in 2019 and was 38.4 in 2024; mortality without documented diabetes declined from 398.7 to 296.6 and was 289.8. In the primary analysis, CVD+DM mortality showed a 13.1% greater relative level increase at 2020 (95% CI, 10.4%-15.9%), with no significant differential change in slope thereafter. Descriptively, the ratio of rate ratios was 1.16, and the absolute difference-in-differences was 5.0 per 100,000. Conclusions: After accounting for cohort-specific pre-2020 trends, CVD mortality with documented diabetes showed a greater relative increase at the 2020 transition. These findings describe differential mortality patterns rather than a causal effect of diabetes or the pandemic. Keywords: Cardiovascular mortality; Diabetes; COVID-19; Difference-in-differences; Preventive Cardiology Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms AAMR: age-adjusted mortality rate APC: annual percentage change CITS: comparative interrupted time-series CVD+DM: cardiovascular disease deaths with diabetes documented as contributing cause DID: differences-in-differences DM: diabetes mellitus

after.authors: Piedboeuf-Potyka, K.; Hering, R.; Schulz, M.; Mackowiak, M.; Brinks, R.; Hoyer, A.; Wirth, M.; Toennies, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Biometrics and Epidemiology, German Diabetes Center (DDZ), Leibniz Center for Diabetes Research at the Heinrich Heine University, 40225 Duesseldor
after.abstract: Background: Current projections of the prevalence and number of persons with type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) are lacking for Germany. This study aims to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. Methods: We used a partial differential equation (PDE) based on the illness-death model to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. The PDE describes the relationship between prevalence, incidence, all-cause mortality and the mortality rate ratio (MRR) of individuals with vs. without type2 diabetes considering age, calendar year and SEP. SEP was measured by quintiles of the German Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation (GISD). Baseline prevalence, incidence, and MRR in 2022 were derived from statutory health insurance data (~85% of the German population). Projected prevalence was multiplied by population projections from the German Federal Statistical Office to estimate the number of persons with diabetes. Results: Type 2 diabetes prevalence increases with age, peaking between 80 and 90 years. Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific prevalence is projected to increase for both sexes across all SEP groups. SEP-related disparities persisted with largest differences between the highest (5th GISD quintile) and lowest (1st GISD quintile) SEP group. The number of persons with type 2 diabetes is projected to rise from 8.4 million in 2022 to between 11.2 and 19.2 million in 2060. Conclusions: Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence is projected to increase with increasing socioeconomic inequalities.

after.title: Preprint: Plasma proteomics reveals signatures of cognitive aging and response to the FINGER multidomain lifestyle intervention
after.authors: Daniilidou, M.; Benedet, A. L.; Solomon, A.; Rosenberg, A.; Morvan, L.; Lehtisalo, J.; Mangialasche, F.; Levalahti, E.; Arslan, B.; Peltonen, M.; Pola, I.; Tan, K.; Ngandu, T.; Zetterberg, H.; Kivipelto, M.; Matton, A.
after.abstract: The FINGER trial demonstrated that a multidomain lifestyle intervention benefits cognition in older adults at-risk of dementia, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We measured neurodegeneration-related proteins using the NULISAseq CNS disease panel in 1158 FINGER participants to investigate associations between circulating proteins, cognitive trajectories, and intervention response. Independent of the intervention, ten proteins spanning immune, neuronal, and metabolic processes were associated with poorer cognitive trajectories, with TREM2 among the strongest signals. The intervention led to changes in eight proteins, including CRH, IL-7 and MME. Eleven proteins modified the cognitive response to intervention, with KDR and CRH showing the strongest effect. Complementary Elastic Net analyses confirmed CRH, and further identified PTN and CCL2 as markers of intervention responsiveness. Additional proteins showed APOE {varepsilon}4- and sex-specific associations with the intervention response. Together, these findings identify proteomic signatures of cognitive response that could inform precision dementia prevention.

after.title: Preprint: Determinants of prices of commercial electric breast pumps sold in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis
after.authors: Gencel-Augusto, J.; Okanmelu, E.; Strobl, F.; Ziebart, M.; Theurich, M.
after.abstract: In Germany, statutory health insurance covers the rental or purchase of breast pumps when a medical indication is present for the mother or infant, and a physician has issued a prescription. However, parents must pay out of pocket for commercially available breast pumps for returning to work or personal circumstances. High indirect costs for continuation of breastfeeding and direct costs for breast pumps and related equipment may pose substantial barriers to breastfeeding families, an issue relevant for health equity. To our knowledge, no studies have assessed the direct financial costs associated with the purchase of commercially available breast pumps. In this cross-sectional study, we examined digital marketplaces in Germany for commercial electric breast pumps between March 2025 and May 2026, across major online platforms. Our objective was to explore pump features that predict price. We identified 282 commercial electric pump models from 108 brands. Basic information was unavailable for half of surveyed breast pump brands. The median price for surveyed commercial electric pumps was 72.70 EUR (IQR: 82.70), with costs ranging widely from 19.99 to 659.57 EUR. Prices varied by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and single user claims; predicting significantly higher costs. Half of pumps surveyed offered only one flange size, signaling additional expenses for mothers needing alternative sizes. These findings highlight important considerations for maternal health and consumer safety. Health technology assessments and a review of current health policy on reimbursement for commercial electric breast pumps is needed

after.title: Preprint: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
after.authors: Li, H.; Li, Y.; Xu, Z.; Pan, W.; Zhao, Z.; Cushing, M.; Wang, F.; Yang, H. S.
after.abstract: Background Laboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. Methods We developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. Findings LabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. Interpretation LabARIA demonstrated the feasibility of coordinating laboratory quality surveillance across heterogeneous data sources, providing a foundation for intelligent clinical laboratories. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether this approach improves monitoring beyond conventional methods, supports laboratory decisions, and benefits patient care without excessive alert burden.

after.title: Preprint: Effect of Data Preprocessing Decisions on Sepsis-3 Labels in MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD: A Sensitivity Analysis
after.authors: Meyer-Eschenbach, F.; v. Stoephasius, J.; Näher, A.-F.; Kohlbacher, F.; Kohler, S.; Grünewald, E.; Frey, N.; Edel, A.; Barrenetxea, J.; Balzer, F.; Kumpf, O.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Medical Informatics, Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Corporate Member of Freie Universität Berlin and Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Berlin,
after.abstract: Objective: Published Sepsis-3 detection rates range from 3.4 % to 65.2 % in MIMIC-III and from 9.8 % to 47.9 % in eICU-CRD. We tested whether data preprocessing decisions alone produce differences of this magnitude when data, cohort and sepsis definition are held fixed. Materials and Methods: Using the MIMIC-III and eICU-CRD databases we developed and applied a configurable pipeline (medalabel) that stepwise maps the databases into the OMOP Common Data Model, standardizes and cleans the data, and preprocesses them to compute Sepsis-3 labels. Each setting of the preprocessing represents one decision of published Sepsis-3 implementations, and settings can be freely combined. On fixed cohorts of first ICU stays (13,388 in MIMIC-III, 94,782 in eICU-CRD), we changed one setting of a reference configuration at a time (51 variants in five preprocessing domains) and compared detection rates and septic stays (Jaccard index) with the reference. We approximately reconstructed six published pipelines and combined the settings with the largest effects in pairs to test whether their effects add up. The time a value is measured can differ from the time it is documented and thus available for automated analysis. Beyond the usual retrospective view based on measurement time, the pipeline optionally combines both time points to simulate a real-time system. Results: The reference configuration labelled 31.5 % of ICU stays in MIMIC-III and 8.2 % in eICU-CRD as septic. Changing a single setting resulted in sepsis detection rates of 15.3-58.6 % in MIMIC-III and 4.6-17.2 % in eICU-CRD. The largest shifts from the reference, all in the same direction in both databases, came from the SOFA baseline, up to +27.1 percentage points (pp) in MIMIC-III and +9.0 pp in eICU-CRD, from disabling imputation (-16.3 and -2.5 pp), the temporal window (+12.6 and +5.3 pp) and aggregation (-10.1 and -0.8 pp); clinician-validated parameter sets had little effect (-4.8 and -1.1 pp). Even variants that changed the rate by less than 2 pp labelled partly different patients, with Jaccard indices as low as 0.67 in MIMIC-III and 0.56 in eICU-CRD (1 = identical septic stays). Reconstructions deviated from the published rates by 2-10 pp. Two settings applied together deviated from the sum of their single effects by 0.9-11.8 pp in MIMIC-III and by up to 4.9 pp in eICU-CRD. Simulating a real-time system lowered the MIMIC-III rate by 5.0 pp and delayed the label in 45 % of the stays that remained septic. Discussion: With the infection criterion held fixed, preprocessing decisions alone can produce a considerable part of the variation between published sepsis detection rates. Similar rates can stem from different patients, which makes studies and prediction models difficult to compare, and retrospective labels rely on values that a real-time system would not yet have. Conclusion: Sepsis-3 labels from health records are only comparable if their data preprocessing is known. Configurable pipelines allow quantifying the effect of these decisions, computing alternative labels on the same data and, in future, validating them against clinician-adjudicated cases.

after.abstract: Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is often underrecognized and undiagnosed. We evaluate the impact of an algorithm-based automatic loading process for CKD in the electronic health record (EHR) problem list at a large health system. Methods Study populations included patients receiving primary or nephrology care at Geisinger (intervention group) and 4 large health systems in the Optum Labs Data Warehouse (OLDW), a longitudinal, real-world data asset with de-identified administrative claims and electronic health record (EHR) data,(comparator group) from 2008-2023. Since 2013, an automated process has been regularly implemented at Geisinger, adding CKD to problem lists of patients meeting laboratory criteria for CKD (outpatient eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 on 2 lab values for [≥] 3 months without intervening normal values). We conducted difference-in-differences (DiD) and difference-in-difference-in-differences (DiDiD) analyses comparing CKD diagnosis rates, CKD-related lab tests, use of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) and statins for those >50 years within 1 year of incident CKD (index date) at Geisinger vs. OLDW health systems before (2008-2012) and after (2013-2023) CKD auto-load implementation. Analyses relied on summary-level data and did not permit adjustment for individual-level characteristics. Results Among patients with incident, undiagnosed CKD (n=21,995 in Geisinger; n=208,402 in OLDW), CKD diagnosis within 1 year of index date increased from 28.4% in 2008-2012 to 65.7% in 2013-2023 at Geisinger whereas CKD diagnosis decreased from 22.6% to 20.7% at OLDW (DiD estimate 39.1%; 95% CI: 38.1%, 40.1%; p<0.001). Among CKD-related labs, DID estimates favored Geisinger for follow-up eGFR, parathyroid hormone, and phosphorus testing (all p values <0.001). CKD auto-load was associated with increased use of RAASi and statins (p values <0.05). Conclusions An algorithm-based problem list auto-load process was associated with higher CKD diagnosis, some CKD-related labs, and use of recommended medications. This scalable strategy should be validated in other health systems.

after.title: Preprint: When will it ever be enough? Black mothers and community advocates perspectives on why evidence of racism in English maternity care does not lead to action: a co-produced focus group study
after.authors: Aryasinghe, S.; Ibuanokpe, S.; Newby-Mayers, R.; Fudlalla, P.; Waithe, C.; Sarpong, G.; Wadhwa, R.; Averill, P.; Das, S.; Ward, H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Patient Experience Research Centre, School of Public Health, Imperial College London
after.abstract: Background: Racism shapes the maternity care and outcomes of Black, African, Caribbean and mixed-Black women in the UK. Services monitor inequities through outcomes and experience data, yet evidence of racism often results in inaction, and existing explanations rely mainly on staff perspectives. We drew on Black mothers and community advocates accounts to explain what stops monitoring of racism from leading to action, and how they propose evidence of racism should be recorded so that it does. Methods: This co-produced qualitative study was underpinned by critical realism and Black feminist thought. Four focus groups were held in London from June to July 2026 with nine Black, African, Caribbean and mixed-Black mothers who used NHS maternity services and seven community advocates. Lived experience co-researchers co-led the study design, data collection and analysis. We used critical realist thematic analysis to propose mechanisms explaining participants accounts, each tested against rival explanations. Results: We propose three mechanisms: credibility discounting, evidence neutralisation and containment of change. Participants described Black womens accounts being discounted until someone else raised the same concern, consistent with testimonial injustice. Recorded evidence appeared to be neutralised through audit culture, as concerns were acknowledged or deflected without action. Change that would shift power or accountability appeared to be contained, consistent with institutional racism. Participants also described harm from staff who shared their racial identity, linked to internalised racism intersecting with language and migration, and to workplace cultures in which Black staff are also dismissed; we interpret this harm as a possible outcome of these mechanisms. Participants proposed that services account for their response to each concern, supported by community-generated evidence, independent observation, qualitative routes and ethnicity-disaggregated data. This would require protection for those who raise concerns and sustained funding and backing for action. Conclusions: Our findings suggest more evidence alone is unlikely to address racism in maternity services. An independently reviewed record of how services respond to each concern could show when they do not act. Change is more likely where services shift power and resources to community organisations working with Black families, while remaining accountable for acting on evidence of racism.

after.authors: Strickland, K. R.; Baird, T.; Burr, L. D.; Dunn, E. M.; Littlejohn, M. L.; Davies, J. L.; Bashford, J. J.; Burke, A.; Evans, I.; Christensen, J.; Brock, J.; McIntosh, L.; Price, E. P.; Sarovich, D. S.
after.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. Methods: P. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. Results: High AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. Conclusions: Our study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.

after.authors: Kubo, A.; Tamura, S.; Hiraide, A.; Fukui, K.; Morioka, D.
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Background: Early defibrillation is the principal modifiable determinant of survival after shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but studies restricted to defibrillated patients cannot observe those who had degenerated before a responder arrived. We quantified this loss and its population-level consequences. Methods: We analysed 368,496 bystander-witnessed adult arrests of presumed cardiac origin in the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2024). Modified Poisson models with marginal standardization estimated the proportion with a shockable rhythm at emergency medical services (EMS) contact and 1-month survival as functions of elapsed time. Assuming exchangeability within strata of bystander category and age, we estimated the additional survivors had patients reached at 15 minutes been reached at 5-10 minutes. Results: The adjusted proportion with a shockable rhythm was 33.1% (95% CI, 30.2-36.5) at 1 minute, 24.7% (24.4-24.9) at 9 minutes and 8.4% (8.0-8.8) at 30 minutes, a relative decline of 4.8% per minute between 5 and 30 minutes. Adjusted 1-month survival fell from 39.5% (38.4-40.6) at 9 minutes to 15.9% (15.1-16.7) at 20 minutes after EMS defibrillation, and from 63.5% (59.9-67.3) at 3 minutes to 47.2% (44.4-50.0) at 10 minutes after bystander defibrillation; each minute cost 2.1 to 2.7 percentage points in both pathways. Shifting the 119,982 patients reached at 15 minutes to 5-10 minutes yielded 6,465 additional survivors (6,259-6,669) over 20 years (323 per year; number needed to treat, 18.6), 59.1% through rhythm preservation. Family-witnessed arrests and the other bystander category, predominantly institutional, accounted for 77.4%. Conclusions: The proportion of patients shockable at EMS contact was approximately 5% lower for each additional minute after collapse, and survival fell by about two percentage points per minute whoever delivered the shock. Under the model's assumptions, most of the benefit of faster contact derives from reaching patients while still shockable, chiefly in arrests witnessed by family members or in institutional settings.

after.abstract: Background. Impaired macrovascular function during acute mental stress predicts adverse events in coronary artery disease, but microvascular stress responses are less understood. Because psychosocial stress and coronary microvascular dysfunction are more common in women, sex differences also warrant study. Methods. We studied individuals aged 18-60 years within 8 months of a myocardial infarction (MI) who underwent a standardized mental stress challenge and were followed for cardiovascular events. We measured peripheral microvascular function with the reactive hyperemia index (RHI) before and after stress; abnormal RHI was defined as [≤]1.67. We also measured brachial flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and myocardial ischemia. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization; a secondary endpoint included recurrent events. Cox regression examined stress-induced RHI decline, adjusting for pre-stress RHI and demographic, clinical, and psychological factors. Results. Among 487 participants (mean age 51 years; 43% women), 89 first and 90 recurrent events occurred over a median 34 months. Women had lower RHI than men before and after stress, and a larger stress-induced decline. Each standard deviation stress-induced RHI decline was associated with 36% higher risk of first events (hazard ratio [HR], 1.36, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01, 1.82) and 44% higher risk of cumulative events (HR, 1.44, 95% CI, 1.04, 2.00), with no significant sex interaction. Abnormal post-stress RHI conferred adjusted HRs of 2.59 (95% CI, 1.13, 5.92) in women and 2.09 (95% CI, 1.11, 3.93) in men; abnormal pre-stress RHI was not predictive (HR, 1.12, 95% CI, 0.71, 1.76). IL-6 and FMD changes and stress-induced ischemia were related to RHI decline but did not explain its association with outcome. Conclusions. Microvascular dysfunction with mental stress is more prevalent in women, and signals an elevated cardiovascular risk after MI in both women and men.

after.title: Preprint: Weighting the weeks that matter: entropic tilting for epidemic forecast evaluation
after.authors: Mathews, J. R.; Lessler, J.; Lemaitre, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
after.abstract: The performance of infectious disease forecasting models is commonly calculated under the implicit assumption that forecast accuracy is equally important across time. This approach may obscure or under-weight differences in model performance during the epidemic periods that matter most for public-health decisions. Here, we introduce the weighted prequential score (WPS), a forecast evaluation framework that can emphasize epidemic periods of interest. The WPS is a weighted average of scores over time, where weights are constructed through entropic tilting which up-weights priority periods while keeping the WPS as close as possible to the arithmetic average. We demonstrate the WPS on forecasts of incident hospitalizations submitted to the CDC FluSight challenge, focusing on two priority periods: weeks of rapid growth in incidence and weeks near the seasonal peak. Across season-location-horizon pairs, doubling the weight assigned to priority periods changes the top-ranked model in 10%-26% of eligible settings, while the top-ranked model remains unchanged regardless of the amount of weight assigned in 37%-68% of settings. We demonstrate that for suitable weights, the models favored by the WPS yield an average gain in accuracy during priority periods that is at least as large as the average accuracy lost during the remaining weeks. Because weights can be defined using observed outcomes, the WPS is not a proper scoring rule. Hence, we recommend using the WPS as a retrospective evaluation diagnostic. The WPS can guide public-health practitioners in selecting models that perform well during periods most relevant to their decisions, while encouraging forecasting teams to improve accuracy during these critical weeks.

after.authors: Gutierrez, S.; Caunca, M. R.; Guo, M.; Hayes-Larson, E.; Milani, S. A.; Gilsanz, P.; Torres, J. M.; Casaletto, K. B.
after.abstract: Importance: Earlier age at menopause associates with increased later life dementia risk, but the biological links that underlie this relationship remain poorly understood in population-based samples. Objective: To evaluate the relationship between history of menopausal timing and AD/ADRD-related blood-based biomarkers in postmenopausal women. Design: Observational study using the U.S. Health and Retirement Study. AD/ADRD-related biomarkers were measured from venous blood draws conducted in 2016 and released in 2025. We estimated linear and nonlinear associations between spontaneous menopause timing and biomarkers, accounting for sociodemographic and health covariates. We evaluated effect modification by APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status. Secondary analyses evaluated associations with hysterectomy history. Setting: Population-based. Participants: Community-dwelling post-menopausal women aged 65 years or older. Exposure: Primary: Self-reported spontaneous age of menopause among women with no history of hysterectomy. Secondary: Self-reported history of hysterectomy (oophorectomy history was not assessed). Main Outcomes and Measures: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) measured in plasma, and phosphorylated tau (p-tau181) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), measured in serum, by Simoa or ELLA. Results: Among 1449 women [≥]65 years, 38.4% self-reported a hysterectomy. Among 893 postmenopausal women without a history of hysterectomy (mean [SD] age at biomarker collection, 75.2 [7.2] years; mean age at menopause, 50.2 [5.2] years), menopausal timing was nonlinearly associated with NfL. Between menopausal ages 45-50, menopause timing was associated with higher NfL (0.010 SD units/year, [95% CI: -0.007, 0.027]), while from menopausal ages 50-55, the association reversed (b= -0.031, [95% CI: -0.051, -0.011]). Associations with GFAP or pTau-181 were not significant, but were directionally similar to those observed for NfL. Later menopausal timing linearly associated with lower GDF-15 (b = -0.015, [95% CI: -0.027, -0.004]). Self-reported hysterectomy was associated with higher GDF-15 (b= 0.118, [95% CI: 0.015, 0.220]), but not other biomarkers. Associations did not significantly differ by APOE {epsilon}4 status. Conclusions and Relevance: In a nationally representative study, earlier age at menopause in midlife was associated with later life AD/ADRDs biomarkers reflecting neuroaxonal degeneration and inflammation, underscoring the importance of understanding reproductive aging in dementia risk.

after.title: Preprint: Smoking trajectories and brain health in middle-aged adults: a 15-year longitudinal study
after.authors: Schuurmans, I. K.; de Ruijter, F.; Wolters, F. J.; Muetzel, R. L.; Franken, I. H. A.; Neitzel, J.; Cousijn, J.; El Marroun, H.
after.abstract: Background. Smoking is a prevalent and preventable risk factor for poor brain health. These habits often establish in early adulthood and have lasting consequences, yet most research focuses on later-life smoking, overlooking important prevention windows. We examined smoking trajectories from early adulthood in relation to midlife brain health. Methods. In 1,900 adults (65.6% female, mean age 32.5 years) from the Dutch population-based Generation R Study (ORACLE subset), smoking was assessed five times over 15 years, from before pregnancy to midlife. K-means clustering identified smoking trajectories, alongside measures of current smoking, pack-years, and abstinence years. At mean age 47.7 years, MRI assessed gray and white matter volumes, white-matter hyperintensity volume, cerebrovascular markers, and vertex-wise cortical thickness and surface area. Findings. Five trajectories were identified: non-smoking (63%), quitting before pregnancy (12%), quitting during/after pregnancy (11%), relapsing (9%), and persistent smoking (4%). All compared with non-smoking, quitting before pregnancy was associated with 6.57 cm3 larger gray matter (95%CI[0.27,12.87],p=.041), 7.71 cm3 larger white matter (95%CI[0.77,14.65],p=.030), and larger cortical surface area in bilateral middle/inferior temporal regions. Quitting during/after pregnancy was associated with more lacunes (OR=2.39; 95%CI[1.23,4.68],p=.011), but similar brain volumes. Relapsing was associated with 0.15 standard deviations more white matter hyperintensity volume (95%CI[0.00,0.30],p=.045) and thinner regions in the right cortex. Persistent smoking had double white matter hyperintensities (0.31 standard deviations; 95%CI[0.10,0.50], p=.003) and widespread bilateral thinner cortices. Similarly, single-timepoint measures like current smoking (vs never smoking) were linked to 9.72 cm3 smaller gray matter volume (95%CI[-16.53,-2.19],p=.005), 0.17 standard deviations more hyperintensity volume (95%CI[0.03,0.32],p=.015), and widespread thinner cortices. Each additional pack-year was associated with 0.45 cm3 smaller gray matter volume (95%CI[-0.85,-0.06],p=.025); each additional abstinence year was associated with 0.01 standard deviations less hyperintensity volume (95%CI[-0.02,0.00],p=.022). Interpretation. Smoking trajectories from early adulthood and midlife are associated with midlife brain health, supporting early and sustained smoking cessation.

after.title: Preprint: Direction of apoB/LDL-C Discordance and Systemic Inflammation in U.S. Adults
after.authors: Kadiri, O.; Esho, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Mercy Health St Elizabeth Youngstown Hospital
after.abstract: Background: Apolipoprotein B (apoB) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) are established biomarkers of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) that tend to be closely correlated. However, some individuals have discordant apoB and LDL-C. We evaluated whether apoB/LDL-C discordance is associated with elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), a key marker of systemic inflammation, in a nationally representative sample. Methods and Results: We analyzed 2226 adults aged 20 years or older from the 2015 to 2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete apoB, LDL-C, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). LDL-C and apoB were converted to survey-weighted scores, and discordance was the residual of apoB regressed on LDL-C. Participants were classified as apoBhigh, LDL-C-high, or concordant (reference). The association of discordance group with elevated hs-CRP (>3 mg/L) was estimated with survey-weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and diabetes. Discordance was present in 26.4% of adults (13.7% apoBhigher, 12.6% LDL-C-higher). Elevated hs-CRP prevalence differed by discordance group: 47.6% (95% CI, 37.6?57.7) in the apoB-high group versus 20.5% (12.9?28.1) in the LDL-C-high group and 33.6% (29.7?37.4) in the concordant group. Relative to concordant participants, adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP were higher for apoB-high discordance (odds ratio [OR], 1.58; 95% CI, 1.03?2.45) and lower for LDL-C-high discordance (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.30?0.78). Similar results were obtained among participants not on statin therapy, with apoB-high discordance demonstrating stronger adjusted odds of elevated hs-CRP (OR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.01?4.04). Conclusion: Discordantly high apoB relative to LDL-C is associated with systemic inflammation in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.

after.title: Preprint: Intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern contraceptive methods among women in sub-Saharan Africa, 1994 to 2024: a multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy
after.authors: Kaonga, P.; Masambi, S.; Nkole, M.; Hazemba, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Zambia Ridgeway Campus: University of Zambia School of Medicine
after.abstract: Background: Demand for family planning satisfied by modern methods is Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 3.7.1, and countries have committed to universal access to family planning by 2030. Inequalities are usually reported one social dimension at a time. This hides how social characteristics combine and leaves open whether programmes should target social groups or strengthen services for all women. We measured intersectional inequalities in demand satisfied by modern methods among women in sub-Saharan Africa over three decades, assessed how well social position discriminates between women, and identified groups left behind. Methods and findings: We did a preregistered cross-sectional analysis of 139 Demographic and Health Surveys from 38 countries with fieldwork from 1994 to 2024. We included 675,584 women aged 15-49 years with demand for family planning and grouped them into 144 intersectional strata by age, union status, education, household wealth and residence. We fitted multilevel logistic models with random effects for strata and surveys (multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy, MAIHDA) and estimated the variance partition coefficient (VPC), the area under the curve (AUC) and the proportional change in variance (PCV). Weighted demand satisfied rose from 27.5% in 1994-99 to 54.1% in 2018-24. Predicted demand satisfied ranged from 13.2% (95% CI: 11.0 - 15.9) among married adolescents with no schooling in the poorest rural households to 68.0% (95% CI: 63.6 - 72.0) among unmarried urban women aged 25-34 years with secondary schooling in the richest households. The strata explained only 6.9% (95% CI: 5.6 - 8.7) of individual variation, with small discriminatory accuracy (AUC = 0.65; 95% CI: 0.63 - 0.66), and a Bayesian model gave a similar VPC (7.0%; 95% credible interval: 5.7 - 8.9). Additive effects explained 95.1% of the between-stratum variance. The VPC fell from 10.1% (95% CI: 8.0 - 12.8) in 1994-99 to 4.5% (95% CI: 3.6 - 5.8) in 2018-24. Five strata of married rural women with no schooling were in the lowest decile in every period. In the latest surveys, married rural women aged 15-24 years with no schooling had lower demand satisfied than other women in 29 of 30 countries (median gap 17.5 percentage points). The 15 most disadvantaged strata held a median 16.4% of unsatisfied demand, so targeting these groups alone would reach about one in six women whose demand is not met. The main limitations are the cross-sectional design, self-reported contraceptive use and the exclusion of 15 early surveys. Conclusions: Intersectional gaps in demand satisfied by modern methods have narrowed in sub-Saharan Africa, and most of the remaining gap between groups is additive. Social position alone discriminates poorly between women, so programmes targeted only by social group would miss most women with unmet need. This supports strengthening universal services. Within universal services, married adolescents and young women with no schooling in poor rural households have been left behind for three decades in almost every country and need priority, country-specific programmes if the 2030 targets are to be met.

after.authors: Kim, S. S.; Wu, E.; Hudgins, A. F.; Crawford, M.; Bruck, M.; Lobelo, F.; Benkeser, D.; Rogawski McQuade, E. T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University
after.abstract: Most nirsevimab effectiveness estimates come from test-negative designs, which restrict populations to those seeking healthcare and testing. We estimated nirsevimab effectiveness among infants six months post-receipt using a target trial emulation with an estimand aligned to phase 3 trials. We emulated a target trial among infants born from February 2, 2023 through May 30, 2026, using electronic medical records at Kaiser Permanente Georgia. Using a g-computation estimator with Cox models fit separately in nirsevimab recipients and non-recipients, we estimated the cumulative incidence of RSV hospitalization and medically-attended RSV at 30-day intervals through 180 days post-receipt. Among 4,826 infants, nirsevimab reduced the risk of RSV hospitalization by 95% (95% CI: 84% to 98%) and medically-attended RSV by 67% (95% CI: 45% to 80%) at 180 days post-receipt. The number needed to immunize to prevent one case was 147 (95% CI: 94 to 333) for RSV hospitalization and 39 (95% CI: 28 to 68) for medically-attended RSV. Nirsevimab was effective through 180 days post-receipt. This cohort-based emulation avoids conditioning on testing and the restricted generalizability of the test-negative and matching-based designs that dominate the literature. These findings support continued nirsevimab use to protect infants against RSV.

after.authors: Presslie, O.; O'Reilly, A.; Zenner, D.; Meghji, J.; Pareek, M.; Cox, S. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: TB Unit, UK Health Security Agency
after.abstract: Background: Linkage of infectious-disease surveillance data to mortality records is important for estimating long-term outcomes, but incomplete personal identifiers present methodological challenges. We developed and validated a deterministic linkage framework for linking the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System (NTBS) with Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality records. Methods: TB notifications in England from 2001 to 2024 were linked to ONS mortality records using 12 sequential matching rules based on combinations of NHS number, date of birth, name, postcode, sex and phonetic matching. Linkage outputs underwent person level deduplication and clerical review. Precision and recall were estimated, and potential linkage bias assessed by variation in identifier completeness and linkage success. Confirmed false-positive links identified during validation were removed from the analytical dataset. Results: Among 151,965 TB notifications, 28,060 initial links were identified. Following deduplication, validation and refinement, 26,937 linked notifications were retained. Estimated precision increased from 97.7% to 99.2% (95% CI 96-100.0) following removal of false-positive links; estimated recall was 98.1% (95% CI 95.4-98.6%). More than 90% of links used NHS-number-based match keys. PDS enrichment increased NHS-number availability and enabled additional NHS-number-based links, although a small proportion linked to different ONS records following enrichment. NHS number availability and linkage success differed across demographic and social groups, demonstrating differential linkage. Conclusions: A hierarchical deterministic approach combined with targeted validation achieved high linkage accuracy while identifying and addressing differential linkage. This provides a transparent framework for future NTBS-ONS linkage and may be adaptable to other surveillance systems where comparable identifiers are available.

Conclusions: A hierarchical deterministic approach combined with targeted validation achieved high linkage accuracy while identifying and addressing differential linkage. We conducted a sex-stratified epigenome-wide association study of newborn saliva DNA methylation in 273 mother-child pairs from the Peruvian Placental Abruption Genetic Epidemiology (PAGE) study. Robust linear regression models adjusted for maternal, cellular, and technical factors identified 318 and 542 ePTB-associated CpG sites and 784 and 1,401 differentially methylated regions in boys and girls, respectively, with limited overlap between sexes. after.title: Preprint: Privilege Is Not Enough: Evaluating Generalized Distillation for Normative Brain Age Modeling in Depression, Anxiety and Alcohol Use Disorder
after.authors: Nitsche, J.; Wiegert, J.; Rezaei, S.; Volkmer, S.; Marty-Lombardi, S.; Gradinger, T.; Streit, F. .; Schwarz, E.
after.abstract: Models trained on rich multimodal data may depend on modalities unavailable at deployment. In generalized distillation, a teacher trained on such privileged data guides a student using only deployable features. We ask whether students inherit clinically meaningful properties beyond predictions in brain-age modeling, where brain-age gaps index deviations from normative aging and brain health. In simulations, distillation recovered a gap-severity association which an age-trained baseline missed. In UK Biobank analyses of depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder, students using structural MRI, functional MRI or biosocial data produced gaps closer to their teacher's than matched baselines in 10 of 12 comparisons. Where teachers most exceeded baselines (anxiety in biosocial, alcohol use in functional MRI students), gap-severity associations rose toward their teacher's. Our findings characterize conditions for successful distillation, i.e. clinical signal the teacher holds, the baseline misses and deployable features contain, and demonstrate their relevance in a real-life psychiatry application.
